# Results — Study 749 (Layoff-Drift)

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The question — **"does a
mass-layoff announcement give a 'restructuring pop', or a longer drift?"** — tested as a
textbook short/long-window **event study**: around each dated layoff announcement, the
**cumulative abnormal return** (CAR) is the stock's return minus a **market-model** fit
(`stock = α + β·SPY`) estimated on a clean pre-event window, cumulated over a short
**pop** window `[+1,+3]` and a longer PEAD-style **drift** window `[+4,+63]`, both entered
one day after the headline. There is no free, survivorship-clean database of layoff dates,
so events come from a **hardcoded, labelled table** of ~28 notable large-cap
announcements, 2015–2025. Offline core + synthetic control are deterministic; run
`python examples/verify.py` to reproduce every number.*

## Data stamp

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Real tape | yfinance daily adjusted closes — each event ticker + SPY (public, no key), **total-return** (auto-adjusted) |
| Event table | hardcoded `LAYOFF_EVENTS` (ticker, announce date, approx. cut), fingerprint **5c784549f0cd** |
| As-of | 2026-07-13 |
| Events in table | **28**; all **28** have usable price history (long-listed large-caps) |
| Benchmark / model | market model `stock = α + β·SPY`, 120-day estimation window, 10-day gap |
| Pop window | CAR **[+1, +3]** trading days (the "restructuring pop") |
| Drift window | CAR **[+4, +63]** trading days (~3 months, the PEAD-style continuation) |
| Entry / costs | **1-day** execution lag throughout (learn intraday, fill next close); one-way 10-bps round-trip |

> **The one caveat that governs the verdict — survivorship, named on the Signal axis.**
> The table is 28 large-caps that **survived to today**. Firms that announced mass layoffs
> *on the way down* and then delisted or were taken under (the distressed restructurings)
> leave no price series and are absent. Selection is on an outcome correlated with the
> post-layoff drift, so the bias points **toward** a positive drift: the sample is, in
> effect, "beaten-down large-caps that recovered." A drift measured here is therefore an
> **upper bound**, not a tradable population law — the whole reason Tradability lands
> `MIRAGE`.

## The two legs — abnormal return around the announcement

| leg | window | n | mean CAR | win-rate | Welch *t* | placebo *p* |
|---|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **pop** ("restructuring pop") | [+1, +3] | 28 | **−0.34%** | 43% | **−0.53** | 0.576 |
| **drift** (PEAD-style) | [+4, +63] | 28 | **+9.01%** | 64% | **+2.25** | **0.007** |

The **pop is dead on arrival**: the market does *not* cheer a layoff on announcement — the
3-day abnormal return is a slightly negative −0.34% (*t* = −0.53), a coin-flip win-rate,
and a placebo *p* of 0.58. The famous "restructuring pop" simply is not there.

The **drift** leg looks alive: +9.01% abnormal over the next quarter (*t* = 2.25, placebo
*p* = 0.007, HAC *t* below). But read the next two sections before believing it.

## The drift's HAC t — and why point-significance is not the end of the story

Pooling the daily abnormal returns over the drift window across all events gives a mean of
**+15.0 bps/day** with a **Newey-West HAC *t* = +3.04** (L = 5, Bartlett). The daily-drift
autocorrelation a genuine PEAD would produce is exactly what the HAC correction is for, and
the point estimate clears the *t* ≥ 2 bar. **On this tape**, there is a positive
post-layoff drift.

## Why it is `WEAK`, not `REAL` — fragility + survivorship

| stress test | result |
|---|--:|
| drop the **3 monster recoveries** (META +55%, XOM +45%, BA +42%) | drift **+4.37%**, *t* = **+1.28** (dies) |
| **bootstrap** the event cross-section (5,000×) | 5th-pct *t* = **+0.73**, median *t* = +2.29 |
| drift **median** (robust to the monsters) | +10.35% |
| collapse **calendar clusters** (13 quarters) | +12.35%, *t* = +2.48 |

The drift is **not** a clustering artifact (it survives collapsing the 12-event Jan–Feb
2023 wave to one observation) and **not** purely two outliers (the median is +10%, and
64% of events drift up). But its *significance* leans on a handful of huge cycle-bottom
recoveries: **drop the top three names and the drift falls to +4.4% at *t* = 1.28**, and a
bootstrap of the cross-section puts the 5th-percentile *t* at **+0.73** — a real share of
resamples are insignificant. Stack that on top of the **survivorship** selection (the
sample is winners by construction) and the honest read is the desk's own definition of
`WEAK`: *significant raw, but fragile to method or selection.*

## Robustness — vary the windows

| pop / drift windows | pop mean | pop *t* | drift mean | drift *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **[+1,+3] / [+4,+63]** (canonical) | −0.34% | −0.53 | +9.01% | +2.25 |
| [0,+1] / [+2,+42] | +0.07% | +0.06 | +6.63% | +2.27 |
| [+1,+5] / [+6,+126] | +0.07% | +0.10 | +18.37% | +2.69 |

The **pop is zero on every window**; the drift is positive on every window but always
resting on the same fragile, survivor-selected cross-section.

## Split — the tech "efficiency wave" vs everything else

| sub-sample | n | pop mean (*t*) | drift mean (*t*) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| 2022+ tech "efficiency wave" | 19 | −0.08% (−0.10) | +9.65% (+2.05) |
| pre-2022 | 9 | −0.89% (−0.73) | +7.65% (+0.97) |

The much-hyped 2022–2024 tech "efficiency" cuts show no more of a pop than the old-economy
cuts, and their drift (+9.7%, *t* = 2.05) is the same beaten-down-survivor recovery as the
rest — it just happens to coincide with the 2023 tech rally.

## The tradable book — cost is *not* the killer

| trade | drift gross | net @ 10 bps |
|---|--:|--:|
| buy +1 day, hold [+4,+63], sell | **+9.01%** | **+8.91%** |

A one-way 10-bps round-trip barely dents the drift — so on *this* sample the book "works."
That is precisely why the honest constraint is not costs but **repeatability**: you cannot
know at the announcement which layoff-announcer becomes META (+55%) and which delists, the
edge evaporates when three recovery names are removed, and the whole thing is a few
macro-timed bear-bottom recoveries wearing a "layoff signal" label.

## Synthetic positive control — the engine is faithful, small samples are weak

A deterministic per-event abnormal-return panel (24 events, seed 723) with **plantable pop
and drift edges**:

| planted pop / drift | pop mean (*t*) | drift mean (*t*) | drift HAC *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| **0 / 0 bps** (no edge) | +0.38% (+0.49) | +4.13% (+0.99) | +1.23 |
| **0 / +400 bps** (large drift) | +0.38% (+0.49) | +8.13% (+1.95) | **+2.42** |

With **no** planted edge neither leg reaches *t* = 2 (the engine does not fabricate
significance from ~two dozen events), and only a large **+400 bps/event** planted drift
pushes the HAC *t* past 2. The control proves the measurement is unbiased **and** that a
two-dozen-event sample only detects a drift when one is genuinely large — so the real-tape
drift, fragile and survivor-flattered, is exactly what a mostly-selection effect looks like
through this keyhole.

## Verdict

- **Signal — WEAK** (compound: **`None` on the pop · `Weak` on the drift**). The
  "restructuring pop" is **absent** (−0.34%, *t* = −0.53, placebo *p* = 0.58). The
  quarter-long drift is nominally significant (+9.01%, Welch *t* = 2.25, HAC *t* = 3.04,
  placebo *p* = 0.007) but **fragile**: drop three cycle-bottom recoveries and it falls to
  +4.4% at *t* = 1.28, the bootstrap 5th-pct *t* is +0.73, and it sits on a
  **survivorship-selected** tape whose bias points straight at this result. Significant
  raw, fragile to selection ⇒ `WEAK`, not `REAL`.
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** Costs are trivial (net +8.91%), so cost is not the constraint —
  **repeatability** is. You cannot pick the survivors ex-ante, the significance rests on a
  few macro-timed recoveries, and the underlying selection ("large-caps that survived their
  layoffs") is unavailable at the moment you would trade.
- **"Restructuring pop?" — BUSTED.** The headline folklore — a stock *cheering* the
  announcement — does not exist (*t* = −0.53). What little drifts up over the next quarter
  is a fragile, survivor-flattered recovery, the opposite of an instant cheer.
